observed.source: whether a Windows program can start from inside
observed.found: A copy of C:\Windows\System32\whoami.exe, which only prints a user name, was placed in the trial user's home and run with a 30 s timeout. Output, verbatim: copied program present: yes | exit code: 1, seconds: 10 | output: [<3>WSL (22 - ) ERROR: UtilAcceptVsock:281: accept4 failed 110] | no Windows user name printed -- the program did not run -- ok | copied program removed: yes. Control: the same program from Ubuntu-20.04, where interop is on, printed 'office\kyu hwan' with exit 0. So Windows programs cannot start from inside the trial distribution. The kernel-wide binfmt registration that still reads 'enabled' is shared with the other distribution and is not what decides it.

observed.source: what the first check got wrong, so the next reader does not repeat it
observed.found: First boot had mounted /mnt/c and /mnt/d. After the change and a restart they were empty folders and not mount points, and they were removed. The first version of the check read the binfmt registration as the verdict; it is a proxy, and the execution test is the measurement. Turning systemd off was a precaution: the registration still read 'enabled' afterwards, so systemd was not what kept it, and the execution test was run after the change. One reading in between was garbled by PowerShell quoting a sh command, and was discarded. Every later step ran from a script file piped through cmd's type.
